title: Why do injuries happen?
summary: NH introduces his injury-prevention series by rejecting the idea of freak injuries: most injuries come from volume and intensity mismanagement or from loading positions your body is not built or prepared for. He gives examples like switching to sumo for unfavorable leverages, dropping weight when changing stance, and his own pec strain from benching cold.
claims: Injuries happen because you failed to control certain variables, not because of bad luck
Injury severity depends on how structurally important the broken part is: a broken nail versus a snapped knee tendon, a finger versus a tibia
The top cause of injury is volume and intensity mismanagement: ego, pushing the intensity too high and forcing the extra rep
His past injuries all came from grinding reps he wasn't capable of; it hasn't happened in close to two years since gaining that wisdom
Bad reps are easier to see coming and survive at higher reps; a rounded-back deadlift at your 8RM is far less risky than at your 1RM
You want the muscles to do the work with minimal tendon, bone, disc and ligament stress; good technique won't save you from a poor loading decision
Volume mistakes produce overuse injuries like tendinitis, usually less severe and preceded by warning signs you chose to ignore

Not everyone can deadlift conventional with a neutral spine even with good mobility; tall lifters with poor leverages often thrive switching to sumo and train hamstrings and lower back with accessories
When changing stance, grip width or introducing a new movement, start light, e.g. a 500 lb squatter narrowing stance should drop to about 250
There are few truly bad positions besides universal faults like flared shoulders or a rounded lumbar spine; lifts like behind-the-neck presses suit some people if approached with respect
Volume/intensity errors and poor positioning cause the vast majority of injuries, which makes injuries highly controllable
Freak injuries are rare; he strained a pec benching one plate after already benching two plates because he hadn't warmed up properly
A third category, like skipping warm-ups or slipping on ice, is still under your control; only things like being tackled mid-lift are truly out of it
